tip: Languages take the definite article in French: comprennent l'espagnol = understand Spanish. English drops the "the," French keeps it.
Adjectives ending in -ent build adverbs in -emment, said like "amman": prudent becomes prudemment = carefully. The double m hides an a-sound.
You don't pay attention in French, you make it: faire attention. Nous faisons attention = we're paying attention. faire covers loads of everyday actions.
French has two "know" verbs. savoir is for facts and info: il sait tout = he knows everything. For people and places you'd switch to connaître.
dépenser is only for spending money or energy, never time. Elle dépense trop = she spends too much (cash). For spending time you'd use passer.
l'addition is the restaurant bill, not a maths sum. Ils partagent l'addition = they split the bill. Say "l'addition, s'il vous plaît" to pay.
encore means "still" here, but also "again" or "more": elle dort encore = she's still asleep. Context picks the meaning.
To cook is literally "to do the kitchen": faire la cuisine. Tu fais la cuisine = you cook. French leans on faire for household chores.
changer de takes a bare noun, no article: change de train = change trains. Same pattern in changer d'avis = change your mind.
des is the plural "some" and can't be dropped: plantez des fleurs = plant (some) flowers. English omits it, French never does.
"Some" before a vowel sound becomes de l', whatever the gender: bois de l'eau = drink (some) water. Before a consonant it splits into du or de la.
After a preposition French uses stressed pronouns: à toi, not "à te." Je pense à toi = I'm thinking of you. Also pour moi, avec lui.
You "pose" a question in French, not ask it: poser une question. Tu poses une question = you ask a question.
réussir = to pass (succeed at). Careful: passer un examen means only to SIT it, not pass it. Elle réussit son examen = she passes her exam.
entendre is hearing that just reaches you; écouter is actively listening. Elle entend un bruit = she hears a noise, unbidden.
raconter is "to tell" a story or events, while dire is to say words. Ils racontent une histoire = they tell a story.
For body parts French uses the article, not "my": je lève la main = I raise my hand (literally "the hand"). Ownership is understood.
présenter means to introduce a person, not "present." Tu présentes ton collègue = you introduce your colleague.
emporter = take something away with you, from here. Ils emportent un parapluie = they take an umbrella along. Bringing toward here is apporter.
pourboire (a tip) is literally "for drink" – pour boire. Je laisse un pourboire = I leave a tip, once money for a drink.
apporter = bring an object toward here; emporter = take it away. Vous apportez le dessert = you bring the dessert. For people, use amener.
louer means both rent AND rent out – tenant and landlord use the same verb. Je loue un appartement = I rent an apartment.
repasser means to iron, but also "to come or pass by again." Il repasse sa chemise = he irons his shirt. Same verb, two lives.
marcher is "to walk," but also "to work/run" for machines: ça marche = it works. Il marche jusqu'à l'école = he walks to school.
un costume is a suit, not a costume (that's un déguisement). Tu portes un costume = you wear a suit.
emprunter = to borrow, but with a road it means to take it: nous empruntons ce chemin = we take this path.
embrasser today means to kiss, not "embrace." Tu embrasses ta grand-mère = you kiss your grandmother, on the cheeks.
gagner means both to win and to earn: il gagne le match = he wins the game, but gagner sa vie = earn a living. Context decides.
You "take" transport with prendre: je prends le train = I take the train. The same verb serves food and drink: prendre un café.
connaître is knowing by familiarity – people, places: elle connaît bien Paris = knows Paris well. For facts you'd switch to savoir.
un roman is a novel, not anything "Roman." Tu lis un roman = you read a novel. A short story is une nouvelle.
French uses the plain present for near-future plans: je pars demain matin = I'm leaving tomorrow morning. No separate "going to" needed.
vivre and habiter both mean "live," but vivre is broader – to be alive, to reside: je vis à Marseille = I live in Marseille.
Most French adjectives follow the noun, but bon comes before: un bon restaurant = a good restaurant. A small set (good, big, old) leads.
For meals prendre means "to have," not take: nous prenons le petit déjeuner = we have breakfast (literally "little lunch").
rester is a false friend: it means to stay, not to rest. Je reste à la maison = I stay home. To rest is se reposer.
avant de + infinitive = "before doing," when it's the same person doing both: avant de parler = before speaking.
Before a plural adjective, des shrinks to de: de bonnes vacances, not "des bonnes." Ils souhaitent de bonnes vacances = they wish happy holidays.
Object pronouns sit before the verb they act on: je peux vous aider = can I help you (literally "you help"). Never trailing after, as in English.
French builds noun compounds with de: un jus d'orange = an orange juice, "juice of orange." The describing noun comes second.
tous les + plural = "every": tous les matins = every morning (literally "all the mornings"). Also tous les jours = every day.
Colours follow the noun in French: une voiture rouge = a red car, literally "a car red." Most descriptive adjectives come after.
Quantity words take de with no article: trop de café = too much coffee, beaucoup de = a lot of. The "some" article drops out.
à + a time means "see you then": à demain = see you tomorrow, à bientôt = see you soon. À demain matin = see you tomorrow morning.
After parler, the language drops its article: je parle français, not "le français." Compare j'apprends le français, which keeps it.
Superlatives use le/la plus + adjective: le plus proche = the nearest. The article repeats: l'hôpital le plus proche = the nearest hospital.
savoir + a verb = "know how to," with no word for "how": je sais nager = I can swim. pouvoir would mean you're merely allowed to.
attendre already means "to wait FOR" – no preposition follows: tu attends le bus = you wait for the bus, never "attends pour."
un pantalon is singular in French though "pants/trousers" is plural in English: ce pantalon = this one pair. Same with un jean.
To get off a vehicle is descendre de: ils descendent du train = they get off the train. Plain descendre alone just means "go down."
Months take en for "in": en juillet = in July, en mars = in March. Nous déménageons en juillet = we move house in July.
allumer = switch on, éteindre = switch off (also to light or put out a fire): tu allumes la lumière = you turn on the light.
